<result># Research Report: Fully-Local Autonomous Coding Pipelines for 30B-Class Models

## 1. Existing fully-local autonomous coding pipelines

**What 30B-class local models actually achieve on real multi-file tasks:**

- **Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B scores 50.3% on SWE-bench Verified** — and notably, a fine-tune of the general Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct matches it at the same 50.3% pass@1. This is the realistic ceiling for your model class with a good scaffold ([Pinggy roundup](https://pinggy.io/blog/best_open_source_self_hosted_llms_for_coding/), [Qwen3-Coder repo](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3-Coder)). Caveat for you: that's the *Coder* variant or a SWE-fine-tune; stock Qwen3-30B-A3B (your reasoning model) will land meaningfully lower on repo-level tasks.
- **Devstral-Small (24B) + OpenHands: 46.8% SWE-bench Verified** (234/500 resolved), beating DeepSeek-V3-0324 and Qwen3-235B-A22B *under the same scaffold*. Mistral and All Hands explicitly built the model around the scaffold — the lesson is that model+harness co-design beats raw parameter count ([OpenHands blog](https://openhands.dev/blog/devstral-a-new-state-of-the-art-open-model-for-coding-agents), [Devstral paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.25193v1), [SWE-bench experiments PR](https://github.com/SWE-bench/experiments/pull/228)).
- **The harness matters as much as the model:** on Terminal-Bench 2.0 the *same model* swings 30–50 percentage points depending on which harness wraps it ([MindStudio analysis](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/best-open-source-llms-agentic-coding-2026)).
- **Aider with local Qwen3-32B: 45.8% on aider polyglot in "whole" edit format with 100% well-formed responses, but only 41.3% in "diff" format with 94.2% well-formed** (17 errors, 14 malformed). Via OpenRouter with default thinking it dropped to 40.0% with 119 error outputs and 12 context exhaustions. Edit-format adherence is a first-order failure mode for sub-70B models; whole-file rewrites are more reliable than diffs ([aider Qwen3 benchmark](https://aider.chat/2025/05/08/qwen3.html), [aider leaderboards](https://aider.chat/docs/leaderboards/)).
- **gpt-engineer / Devika with local models:** essentially no quantitative success data exists. gpt-engineer's own docs frame local models as "catching up" with degradation from quantization; Devika recommends Claude 3 "for optimal performance" and publishes no local-model numbers. An empirical failure study found open models show the same failure classes as closed ones *plus extra parsing breakdowns* ([gpt-engineer open models doc](https://gpt-engineer.readthedocs.io/en/latest/open_models.html), [Devika repo](https://github.com/stitionai/devika), [failure study](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.13655)).
- **smolagents (HuggingFace):** their CodeAgent design (agent writes actions as Python code, not JSON tool calls) uses ~30% fewer steps/LLM calls and scores higher on hard benchmarks; open models matched proprietary ones on their GAIA-derived suite ([smolagents blog](https://huggingface.co/blog/smolagents), [structured CodeAgent blog](https://huggingface.co/blog/structured-codeagent), [beating GAIA](https://huggingface.co/blog/beating-gaia)).

**Scaffolding that compensates for weak models:** hierarchical localization before editing, whole-file edit formats, constrained single-purpose phases, generated-test validation of candidate patches, strict output-format retry loops, and tool access (which helps small models far more than "thinking" does — see section 4).

## 2. TDD-loop agents and execution feedback

- **Tests-in-prompt measurably helps:** Mathews & Nagappan, "Test-Driven Development for Code Generation" ([arXiv 2402.13521](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.13521)) — giving GPT-4 the tests alongside the problem statement: MBPP 69.67% → 82.45% (+12.8 pts), HumanEval 78.66% → 87.81% (+9.2 pts), CodeChef 23.0% → 26.1%. Effect replicated on Llama 3. Writing/locking tests *before* implementation is empirically the right ordering, not just discipline.
- **Execution feedback beats single-shot, especially via iteration:** "How Many Tries Does It Take? Iterative Self-Repair Across Model Scales" ([arXiv 2604.10508](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.10508)) tested Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 32B, Llama 3.3 70B, and others with up to 5 repair attempts fed execution errors: **+4.9 to +17.1 pts on HumanEval, +16.0 to +30.0 pts on MBPP — gains universal across scales, and current instruction-tuned small models no longer need fine-tuning to self-repair. Most gains concentrate in the first two repair rounds.** This is the strongest direct evidence that your RED-GREEN loop with pytest as verifier is the correct architecture for a 30B model, and that a repair cap of 2–3 rounds captures most of the value.
- The lineage: Self-Debugging ([arXiv 2304.05128](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.05128)) established unit-test execution feedback as the strongest feedback signal; a test-execution agent providing feedback reached 89.9% on MBPP in a multi-agent setup ([survey, arXiv 2408.02479](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.02479)).
- **Counterpoint to watch:** "Rethinking the Value of Agent-Generated Tests" ([arXiv 2602.07900](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.07900v2)) finds that when the *agent writes its own tests mid-task*, test-writing intensity only weakly correlates with task success, and agents drift to print-based observation over assertions. Implication: the value is in tests generated in a *dedicated, gated phase* and then frozen as the verifier — exactly your deterministic-gate design — not in letting the agent freestyle tests during implementation.
- A TDD benchmark now exists: "Tests as Prompt" ([arXiv 2505.09027](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.09027v1)) if you want an eval target.

## 3. Self-consistency / multi-sample voting for agent steps

- **For final code artifacts: clearly worth it, if you vote with execution.** CodeT ([arXiv 2207.10397](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.10397)) — sample N solutions + N generated tests, score by dual execution agreement: HumanEval pass@1 47.0% → 65.8% (+18.8 absolute) on code-davinci-002, consistent gains across five models including small ones. Functional Majority Voting (clustering candidates by runtime execution signatures) shows similar boosts ([Majority Voting for Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.15618)). Agentless itself samples multiple candidate patches and selects via regression tests ([arXiv 2407.01489](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01489)).
- **For intermediate agent steps: mostly not worth it.** Sophisticated selection methods often fail to beat plain self-consistency once inference cost is counted, and LLM-as-judge selection (Universal Self-Consistency) adds ~10% inference time and ~15% memory for marginal gain ([Latent Self-Consistency](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.18395), [Self-Certainty best-of-N](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.18581)). Plain textual majority voting also doesn't apply cleanly to free-form agent actions (no canonical answer to vote on).
- **Practical rule for single-stream local inference (your MLX setup, where N samples = N× wall-clock):** spend samples only where a cheap deterministic verifier exists (does the patch apply? do tests pass? does JSON validate?) — i.e., best-of-N with execution filtering at the patch level — and run all other steps greedily. Voting on *enum-output* steps (classify/triage with Gemma) is cheap and reasonable; voting on reasoning steps is not.

## 4. Pipeline-of-small-steps vs monolithic agent

- **Agentless ([arXiv 2407.01489](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01489))** is the canonical result: a fixed three-phase pipeline (hierarchical localization → repair with multiple candidate diffs → test-based patch validation), no agent autonomy, no tool choice — beat every open-source *agent* on SWE-bench Lite at the time (32.0%) at $0.70/issue. OpenAI adopted it as their reference scaffold for GPT-4o and o1. The weaker the model, the stronger the argument for taking action-selection away from it.
- **Decomposed prompting beats monolithic prompts broadly:** gains of +4.2 to +12.9 pts on math/multi-hop benchmarks; decomposed 50.6% vs CoT 36% EM in one comparison ([EmergentMind survey of prompted decomposition](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/llm-based-prompted-decomposition)).
- **"Can Small Agent Collaboration Beat a Single Big LLM?" ([arXiv 2601.11327](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.11327v1))**, Qwen3 4B–32B on GAIA: a 4B model *with tools* (18.2%) beat a 32B model *without* (12.7%); tool augmentation gave the largest, most consistent gains for small models. Critical finding for you: **full "thinking" mode frequently *degraded* agentic performance** — causing tool omission, looping/non-termination, and format drift (4B agentic accuracy fell 13.3% → 9.1% with thinking on). Best results came from thinking applied *only to the planning role*, not uniformly.
- smolagents' 30% step reduction from code-actions and the aider diff-format data above reinforce the same theme: every degree of freedom you remove from a sub-70B model (output format, action space, phase ordering) converts directly into reliability.

## Five most actionable recommendations for datum-local

1. **Keep the deterministic-gate pipeline; shrink the agent's autonomy further, Agentless-style.** Replace any "figure out what to do" agentic step with fixed phases: hierarchical localization (files → functions → edit sites) as its own model call, then constrained editing. Agentless beat full agents on SWE-bench Lite with exactly this shape, and the 30–50 pt harness swing on Terminal-Bench says your scaffold is worth more than a model upgrade.

2. **Cap the RED-GREEN repair loop at 2–3 iterations per failure, then escalate or re-plan.** Execution-feedback repair gives +16 to +30 pts on MBPP-class tasks for models like Qwen3-32B, but most of the gain lands in rounds 1–2; beyond that you're burning MLX wall-clock on a model talking itself in circles. Make "3 strikes → regenerate from plan" a gate rule.

3. **Generate and freeze tests in a dedicated gated phase; never let the implementation agent author or modify the verifier.** Tests-in-prompt is worth +9 to +13 pts (Mathews & Nagappan), but agent-written mid-task tests correlate only weakly with success and degrade into print-debugging. Your gate should hash the test files at RED and reject any diff touching them during GREEN.

4. **Use whole-file edit format, not unified diffs, for Qwen3-30B writes.** Qwen3-32B drops 45.8% → 41.3% and loses ~6% well-formedness switching whole → diff on aider polyglot. For files under your 500-line cap, full-file rewrite + git diff computed deterministically afterwards is strictly more reliable. Also disable thinking mode inside tool-loop steps and enable it only for the planning phase — thinking measurably degrades small-model tool execution (looping, format drift).

5. **Spend your sampling budget on best-of-N patches filtered by test execution — nowhere else.** CodeT-style execution-agreement selection is worth ~19 pts; voting on intermediate reasoning steps is not worth single-stream MLX latency. Concretely: sample 3–5 candidate implementations at temperature ~0.7 at the GREEN step, run the frozen test suite against each, take the first/most-agreeing passer. Gemma extraction steps with enum outputs can use cheap 3-vote majority; everything else runs greedy.

One strategic note: stock Qwen3-30B-A3B is your reasoning model, but the SWE-tuned variants (Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, or the 50.3% fine-tune of your exact base) are the same memory footprint with materially better repo-level editing — worth a swap for the implementation phase while keeping the base model for planning.</result>

<result># Research Report: Fully-Local Autonomous Coding Pipelines for 30B-Class Models

## 1. Existing fully-local autonomous coding pipelines

**What 30B-class local models actually achieve on real multi-file tasks:**

- **Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B scores 50.3% on SWE-bench Verified** — and notably, a fine-tune of the general Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct matches it at the same 50.3% pass@1. This is the realistic ceiling for your model class with a good scaffold ([Pinggy roundup](https://pinggy.io/blog/best_open_source_self_hosted_llms_for_coding/), [Qwen3-Coder repo](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3-Coder)). Caveat for you: that's the *Coder* variant or a SWE-fine-tune; stock Qwen3-30B-A3B (your reasoning model) will land meaningfully lower on repo-level tasks.
- **Devstral-Small (24B) + OpenHands: 46.8% SWE-bench Verified** (234/500 resolved), beating DeepSeek-V3-0324 and Qwen3-235B-A22B *under the same scaffold*. Mistral and All Hands explicitly built the model around the scaffold — the lesson is that model+harness co-design beats raw parameter count ([OpenHands blog](https://openhands.dev/blog/devstral-a-new-state-of-the-art-open-model-for-coding-agents), [Devstral paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.25193v1), [SWE-bench experiments PR](https://github.com/SWE-bench/experiments/pull/228)).
- **The harness matters as much as the model:** on Terminal-Bench 2.0 the *same model* swings 30–50 percentage points depending on which harness wraps it ([MindStudio analysis](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/best-open-source-llms-agentic-coding-2026)).
- **Aider with local Qwen3-32B: 45.8% on aider polyglot in "whole" edit format with 100% well-formed responses, but only 41.3% in "diff" format with 94.2% well-formed** (17 errors, 14 malformed). Via OpenRouter with default thinking it dropped to 40.0% with 119 error outputs and 12 context exhaustions. Edit-format adherence is a first-order failure mode for sub-70B models; whole-file rewrites are more reliable than diffs ([aider Qwen3 benchmark](https://aider.chat/2025/05/08/qwen3.html), [aider leaderboards](https://aider.chat/docs/leaderboards/)).
- **gpt-engineer / Devika with local models:** essentially no quantitative success data exists. gpt-engineer's own docs frame local models as "catching up" with degradation from quantization; Devika recommends Claude 3 "for optimal performance" and publishes no local-model numbers. An empirical failure study found open models show the same failure classes as closed ones *plus extra parsing breakdowns* ([gpt-engineer open models doc](https://gpt-engineer.readthedocs.io/en/latest/open_models.html), [Devika repo](https://github.com/stitionai/devika), [failure study](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.13655)).
- **smolagents (HuggingFace):** their CodeAgent design (agent writes actions as Python code, not JSON tool calls) uses ~30% fewer steps/LLM calls and scores higher on hard benchmarks; open models matched proprietary ones on their GAIA-derived suite ([smolagents blog](https://huggingface.co/blog/smolagents), [structured CodeAgent blog](https://huggingface.co/blog/structured-codeagent), [beating GAIA](https://huggingface.co/blog/beating-gaia)).

**Scaffolding that compensates for weak models:** hierarchical localization before editing, whole-file edit formats, constrained single-purpose phases, generated-test validation of candidate patches, strict output-format retry loops, and tool access (which helps small models far more than "thinking" does — see section 4).

## 2. TDD-loop agents and execution feedback

- **Tests-in-prompt measurably helps:** Mathews & Nagappan, "Test-Driven Development for Code Generation" ([arXiv 2402.13521](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.13521)) — giving GPT-4 the tests alongside the problem statement: MBPP 69.67% → 82.45% (+12.8 pts), HumanEval 78.66% → 87.81% (+9.2 pts), CodeChef 23.0% → 26.1%. Effect replicated on Llama 3. Writing/locking tests *before* implementation is empirically the right ordering, not just discipline.
- **Execution feedback beats single-shot, especially via iteration:** "How Many Tries Does It Take? Iterative Self-Repair Across Model Scales" ([arXiv 2604.10508](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.10508)) tested Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 32B, Llama 3.3 70B, and others with up to 5 repair attempts fed execution errors: **+4.9 to +17.1 pts on HumanEval, +16.0 to +30.0 pts on MBPP — gains universal across scales, and current instruction-tuned small models no longer need fine-tuning to self-repair. Most gains concentrate in the first two repair rounds.** This is the strongest direct evidence that your RED-GREEN loop with pytest as verifier is the correct architecture for a 30B model, and that a repair cap of 2–3 rounds captures most of the value.
- The lineage: Self-Debugging ([arXiv 2304.05128](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.05128)) established unit-test execution feedback as the strongest feedback signal; a test-execution agent providing feedback reached 89.9% on MBPP in a multi-agent setup ([survey, arXiv 2408.02479](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.02479)).
- **Counterpoint to watch:** "Rethinking the Value of Agent-Generated Tests" ([arXiv 2602.07900](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.07900v2)) finds that when the *agent writes its own tests mid-task*, test-writing intensity only weakly correlates with task success, and agents drift to print-based observation over assertions. Implication: the value is in tests generated in a *dedicated, gated phase* and then frozen as the verifier — exactly your deterministic-gate design — not in letting the agent freestyle tests during implementation.
- A TDD benchmark now exists: "Tests as Prompt" ([arXiv 2505.09027](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.09027v1)) if you want an eval target.

## 3. Self-consistency / multi-sample voting for agent steps

- **For final code artifacts: clearly worth it, if you vote with execution.** CodeT ([arXiv 2207.10397](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.10397)) — sample N solutions + N generated tests, score by dual execution agreement: HumanEval pass@1 47.0% → 65.8% (+18.8 absolute) on code-davinci-002, consistent gains across five models including small ones. Functional Majority Voting (clustering candidates by runtime execution signatures) shows similar boosts ([Majority Voting for Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.15618)). Agentless itself samples multiple candidate patches and selects via regression tests ([arXiv 2407.01489](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01489)).
- **For intermediate agent steps: mostly not worth it.** Sophisticated selection methods often fail to beat plain self-consistency once inference cost is counted, and LLM-as-judge selection (Universal Self-Consistency) adds ~10% inference time and ~15% memory for marginal gain ([Latent Self-Consistency](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.18395), [Self-Certainty best-of-N](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.18581)). Plain textual majority voting also doesn't apply cleanly to free-form agent actions (no canonical answer to vote on).
- **Practical rule for single-stream local inference (your MLX setup, where N samples = N× wall-clock):** spend samples only where a cheap deterministic verifier exists (does the patch apply? do tests pass? does JSON validate?) — i.e., best-of-N with execution filtering at the patch level — and run all other steps greedily. Voting on *enum-output* steps (classify/triage with Gemma) is cheap and reasonable; voting on reasoning steps is not.

## 4. Pipeline-of-small-steps vs monolithic agent

- **Agentless ([arXiv 2407.01489](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01489))** is the canonical result: a fixed three-phase pipeline (hierarchical localization → repair with multiple candidate diffs → test-based patch validation), no agent autonomy, no tool choice — beat every open-source *agent* on SWE-bench Lite at the time (32.0%) at $0.70/issue. OpenAI adopted it as their reference scaffold for GPT-4o and o1. The weaker the model, the stronger the argument for taking action-selection away from it.
- **Decomposed prompting beats monolithic prompts broadly:** gains of +4.2 to +12.9 pts on math/multi-hop benchmarks; decomposed 50.6% vs CoT 36% EM in one comparison ([EmergentMind survey of prompted decomposition](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/llm-based-prompted-decomposition)).
- **"Can Small Agent Collaboration Beat a Single Big LLM?" ([arXiv 2601.11327](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.11327v1))**, Qwen3 4B–32B on GAIA: a 4B model *with tools* (18.2%) beat a 32B model *without* (12.7%); tool augmentation gave the largest, most consistent gains for small models. Critical finding for you: **full "thinking" mode frequently *degraded* agentic performance** — causing tool omission, looping/non-termination, and format drift (4B agentic accuracy fell 13.3% → 9.1% with thinking on). Best results came from thinking applied *only to the planning role*, not uniformly.
- smolagents' 30% step reduction from code-actions and the aider diff-format data above reinforce the same theme: every degree of freedom you remove from a sub-70B model (output format, action space, phase ordering) converts directly into reliability.

## Five most actionable recommendations for datum-local

1. **Keep the deterministic-gate pipeline; shrink the agent's autonomy further, Agentless-style.** Replace any "figure out what to do" agentic step with fixed phases: hierarchical localization (files → functions → edit sites) as its own model call, then constrained editing. Agentless beat full agents on SWE-bench Lite with exactly this shape, and the 30–50 pt harness swing on Terminal-Bench says your scaffold is worth more than a model upgrade.

2. **Cap the RED-GREEN repair loop at 2–3 iterations per failure, then escalate or re-plan.** Execution-feedback repair gives +16 to +30 pts on MBPP-class tasks for models like Qwen3-32B, but most of the gain lands in rounds 1–2; beyond that you're burning MLX wall-clock on a model talking itself in circles. Make "3 strikes → regenerate from plan" a gate rule.

3. **Generate and freeze tests in a dedicated gated phase; never let the implementation agent author or modify the verifier.** Tests-in-prompt is worth +9 to +13 pts (Mathews & Nagappan), but agent-written mid-task tests correlate only weakly with success and degrade into print-debugging. Your gate should hash the test files at RED and reject any diff touching them during GREEN.

4. **Use whole-file edit format, not unified diffs, for Qwen3-30B writes.** Qwen3-32B drops 45.8% → 41.3% and loses ~6% well-formedness switching whole → diff on aider polyglot. For files under your 500-line cap, full-file rewrite + git diff computed deterministically afterwards is strictly more reliable. Also disable thinking mode inside tool-loop steps and enable it only for the planning phase — thinking measurably degrades small-model tool execution (looping, format drift).

5. **Spend your sampling budget on best-of-N patches filtered by test execution — nowhere else.** CodeT-style execution-agreement selection is worth ~19 pts; voting on intermediate reasoning steps is not worth single-stream MLX latency. Concretely: sample 3–5 candidate implementations at temperature ~0.7 at the GREEN step, run the frozen test suite against each, take the first/most-agreeing passer. Gemma extraction steps with enum outputs can use cheap 3-vote majority; everything else runs greedy.

One strategic note: stock Qwen3-30B-A3B is your reasoning model, but the SWE-tuned variants (Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, or the 50.3% fine-tune of your exact base) are the same memory footprint with materially better repo-level editing — worth a swap for the implementation phase while keeping the base model for planning.</result>

<result># Research Report: Grammar-Constrained Decoding, Tiny-Model Tool Extraction, Agent Context Management, and Qwen3-30B-A3B

## 1. Does grammar-constrained decoding hurt reasoning? Does research validate freeform-then-extract?

**Short answer: yes, your two-stage architecture is the pattern the literature converged on — but the nuance matters.**

- **"Let Me Speak Freely?" (Tam et al., arXiv:2408.02442, EMNLP 2024 Industry)** found a significant decline in reasoning ability under format restrictions, with **stricter constraints causing greater degradation** (constrained JSON-mode worst, format-instructions milder). Two findings directly relevant to you: (a) **classification/extraction tasks were unhurt or improved** by structure — constraints reduce ambiguity there; (b) their **NL-to-Format mitigation — generate the answer in natural language first, then convert to the target format in a second pass — recovers most of the loss** by "decoupling content generation from formatting." That is exactly your Qwen-thinks / Gemma-extracts split. ([arxiv.org/abs/2408.02442](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.02442), [emergentmind.com/papers/2408.02442](https://www.emergentmind.com/papers/2408.02442))
- **The .txt (dottxt) rebuttal "Say What You Mean"** showed the original result was partly an artifact: with identical prompts, the schema actually shown in the prompt, and a reasoning field placed *before* the answer field, structured generation matched or beat unstructured (GSM8K 0.78 vs 0.77, Last Letter 0.77 vs 0.73, Shuffle Objects 0.44 vs 0.41). Their prescriptions: put the schema and an example in the prompt, give the model a bounded `reasoning` field first, constrain the answer field with enums/regex. ([blog.dottxt.ai/say-what-you-mean.html](https://blog.dottxt.ai/say-what-you-mean.html))
- **JSONSchemaBench (arXiv:2501.10868, "Generating Structured Outputs from Language Models")** tested Guidance, Outlines, llama.cpp, **XGrammar**, OpenAI, Gemini: with adequate prompting, constrained decoding *improved* downstream accuracy (+3.3 to +3.7 pp on Last Letter / Shuffle Objects / GSM8K) and sped up generation ~50%. Quality loss is driven by **poor schema/prompt design, not the constraint mechanism itself**. ([arxiv.org/html/2501.10868v1](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.10868v1))
- **CRANE (ICML 2025, arXiv:2502.09061)** supplies the theory: restricting output to a grammar containing *only* final answers provably reduces model expressivity (no room for intermediate computation); augmenting the grammar with a free reasoning region restores it. Alternating unconstrained reasoning with constrained answer emission gained **up to 10 pp** on GSM-Symbolic/FOLIO over both pure-constrained and pure-unconstrained decoding. ([arxiv.org/abs/2502.09061](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.09061)) Follow-on 2025-26 work (DCCD, Lookahead-then-Verify for diffusion LLMs) continues this "constrain the answer, not the thinking" line. ([aclanthology.org/2025.acl-industry.34](https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-industry.34/))

**Synthesis:** the field agrees that *reasoning must happen outside the grammar*; it disagrees only on whether that free region lives inside one constrained generation (CRANE, dottxt's reasoning-field-first) or in a separate pass (Tam's NL-to-Format = your pipeline). Your extraction step is a classification/extraction task — precisely the category where constraints **help**, per both Tam et al. and JSONSchemaBench. Architecture validated.

## 2. Tool-call extraction with tiny models (<8B)

- **BFCL scale check:** Llama 3.1 8B-Instruct scores ~76% on the AST-era leaderboard vs 88.5% for 405B; on the harder BFCL v3 (multi-turn included), even leaders sit at ~76% (GLM-4.5 76.7, Qwen3-32B 75.7) — small models fall off a cliff on multi-turn. Gemma 3 1B scores ~31% BFCL. ([gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/blogs/8_berkeley_function_calling_leaderboard.html](https://gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/blogs/8_berkeley_function_calling_leaderboard.html), [llm-stats.com/benchmarks/bfcl](https://llm-stats.com/benchmarks/bfcl), [pricepertoken.com/leaderboards/benchmark/bfcl-v3](https://pricepertoken.com/leaderboards/benchmark/bfcl-v3))
- **Docker's practical local eval (21 models, 3,570 cases, M4 Max):** Qwen3-14B F1 0.971, **Qwen3-8B 0.933**, Llama 3.1 8B 0.835, **Gemma 3 4B 0.733**. Dominant failure modes, in order: **(1) eager invocation** (tool call on a greeting), **(2) wrong tool selection**, **(3) invalid/missing arguments**, **(4) ignoring tool responses**. Quantization had no significant effect on tool-call accuracy. Note the compounding math: 95% per-step accuracy → ~66% over an 8-step loop. ([docker.com/blog/local-llm-tool-calling-a-practical-evaluation](https://www.docker.com/blog/local-llm-tool-calling-a-practical-evaluation/))
- **Hammer (arXiv:2410.04587):** small models are **misled by function/parameter names** (they pattern-match names instead of reading descriptions) and are weak at **irrelevance detection** (knowing when *no* tool applies). Function-name masking plus irrelevance-augmented training let 1.5-7B models beat much larger ones. ([arxiv.org/abs/2410.04587](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.04587))
- **FunctionGemma (Gemma 270M fine-tune)** jumped 58% → 85% on a narrow mobile-actions domain after task-specific fine-tuning — tiny models do fine when the decision space is small and in-domain. ([blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/functiongemma](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/functiongemma/))

**Implication for your split:** Gemma-E4B as a *deciding* agent would be ~0.73 F1 territory. But you're not asking it to decide — Qwen already decided in freeform; Gemma only maps prose to schema. That reframes the task from function-calling (hard for 4B) to constrained extraction (easy for 4B). The residual risks are the known small-model ones: name-similarity confusion between tools and malformed args.

## 3. Multi-turn context management on small budgets

- **"The Complexity Trap" (arXiv:2508.21433, JetBrains Research):** on SWE-bench-style agents, **simple observation masking — keep full observations for the last M=10 turns, replace older observations with a one-line placeholder ("Previous N lines omitted"), keep ALL reasoning and action tokens — matches or beats LLM summarization at roughly half the cost** (Qwen3-Coder 480B: 53.8% raw → 54.8% masked; 50-57% cost reduction). They tested **Qwen3-32B** (closest published datapoint to your 30B-A3B): masking and summarization performed similarly, summarization marginally cheaper there. Key trap: summaries **mask failure signals**, so agents persist in dead ends longer, inflating trajectories and cost. ([arxiv.org/abs/2508.21433](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.21433), [blog.jetbrains.com/research/2025/12/efficient-context-management](https://blog.jetbrains.com/research/2025/12/efficient-context-management/))
- **Framework practice:** SWE-agent ships observation masking (old observations elided, recent kept; failed retry turns skipped). OpenHands uses an LLM condenser that fires when history exceeds `max_size` and replaces dropped events with a generated summary — works, but inherits the failure-signal-masking problem and needs a second model call. ([docs.openhands.dev/sdk/guides/context-condenser](https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/guides/context-condenser))
- **Scaffold-dependence caveat:** which strategy wins depends on what your scaffold keeps.     """Static per-run system prompt: role, tool catalog, code rules.

    Stable across turns so the inference server's prefix cache can reuse it.
    Kept to ~6 rules — instruction-following degrades with rule count on
    small models.
    """
    return (
        "You are a coding agent working inside a repository. "
        "You accomplish tasks by calling tools, one per step.\n\n"
        f"TOOLS (name, args, purpose):\n{_catalog_lines(allowed_tools)}\n\n"
        "RULES:\n"
        "1. Read a file before you overwrite it (enforced).\n"
        "2. When writing a file, output the COMPLETE file content in one "
        "fenced code block (```...```), then name the tool and path.\n"
        "3. After a successful write, never rewrite the same file — verify "
        "with run_command or declare DONE.\n"
        "4. Update any comment or docstring your change makes false.\n"
        "5. Match the existing code style; make the smallest change that "
        "accomplishes the task; no new files unless the task requires them.\n"
        "6. Never remove existing tests or functions unless the task says so.\n\n"
        "End every response with exactly one line:\n"
        "NEXT: <tool_name> <json args without file content> | NEXT: DONE"
    )

def agent_loop(task: str, config: dict, phase: str = "agent", on_step=None) -> dict:
    """Run the ReAct loop until done, max_steps, timeout, or loop detection.

    on_step, if given, is called with each completed step dict (thought,
    tool_name, tool_args, observation) — for live progress reporting.

    Returns {"result": {"summary": str} | None, "escalated": bool,
             "reason": str | None, "phase": str, "steps_taken": int,
             "steps": list, "total_tokens": int, "total_time_s": float}.
    """
    base = load_config()
    think_model = config.get("think_model") or base.get("model")
    decide_model = (
        config.get("decide_model")
        or base.get("fast_model")
        or get_model_for_phase(phase)
    )
    max_steps = config.get("max_steps", 10)
    timeout_s = config.get("timeout_s", 600)
    think_max_tokens = config.get("think_max_tokens", 2048)
    allowed_tools = config.get("allowed_tools", list(TOOL_CATALOG))

    history: list[dict] = []
    total_tokens = 0
    start = time.monotonic()
    recent_signatures: list[str] = []
    read_paths: set[str] = set()

    def _finish(summary: str | None, escalated: bool, reason: str | None) -> dict:
        return {
            "result": {"summary": summary} if summary is not None else None,
            "escalated": escalated,
            "reason": reason,
            "phase": phase,
            "steps_taken": len(history),
            "steps": history,
            "total_tokens": total_tokens,
            "total_time_s": round(time.monotonic() - start, 2),
        }

    for _step in range(max_steps):
        if time.monotonic() - start >= timeout_s:
            return _finish(None, True, "timeout_exceeded")

        # ── THINK (main model, freeform) ─────────────────────────────────
        think_prompt = _build_think_prompt(task, history, allowed_tools)
        think_out = _think(think_prompt, think_model, think_max_tokens)
        total_tokens += think_out.get("tokens", 0)
        thought = _strip_think_tags(think_out.get("text", ""))

        # ── DECIDE (fast model, structured) ──────────────────────────────
        decide_prompt = _build_decide_prompt(thought, allowed_tools)
        decide_out = _decide(decide_prompt, decide_model)
        total_tokens += decide_out.get("tokens", 0)
        decision = decide_out.get("data") or {}

        if decision.get("action") == "done":
            history.append(
                {
                    "thought": thought,
                    "tool_name": "done",
                    "tool_args": {},
                    "observation": decision.get("summary", ""),
                }
            )
            if on_step:
                on_step(history[-1])
            return _finish(decision.get("summary", ""), False, None)

        tool_name = decision.get("tool_name", "")

        # ── ASSEMBLE (Python boundary) ───────────────────────────────────

content.text:
Run 4 is live — first full RED-GREEN-REFACTOR. Now your three questions, answered properly:

**Context window — can it be 128K? Yes, but it isn't today, and three layers were lying about it.** Our `Qwen3-30B-A3B` (original hybrid) is **32K native**; 128K requires enabling YaRN rope scaling (factor 4) in the model's `config.json`. On top of that, oMLX itself clamps at `max_context_window: 32768` in its settings, and datum's `max_kv_size: 32768` rotating buffer caps attention anyway. So our old config claiming 262144 was fiction at every layer — I set it to an honest 32768. If M3/M4 (whole-diff review on real repos) needs more, the upgrade path is: YaRN in the model config + raise oMLX's clamp + raise `max_kv_size` — KV cost at 128K is roughly ~6GB at 8-bit, which fits. But Qwen's own guidance is static YaRN slightly degrades short-context quality, so don't pay for it until something actually needs >32K. With observation masking, M1 runs peaked around 2-3K tokens.

**KV cache — it wasn't set up, now it is.** Two different things here:
- *KV quantization* (`kv_bits=8`): only applies on the direct mlx_lm path; we route through oMLX, which manages its own KV.
- *Prefix cache* (the one that matters for our loop): oMLX had `ssd_cache_dir: null` and `hot_cache_max_size: "0"` — disabled. Every THINK turn re-prefilled the entire prompt from token zero. Now: **50GB SSD cache on `/Volumes/Extra/omlx-cache`** (not the boot drive) + **4GB in-memory hot cache**, service restarted. Since our prompts share a stable prefix (system prompt + task, history only appended), later turns should prefill nearly instantly.

**System prompt — didn't exist, now it does.** Everything used to ride in a single user message. Now `generate()` supports a proper system role, and the agent loop puts the static content there — role, tool catalog, and exactly **6 code rules** (read-before-write, complete-file fenced blocks, never rewrite after success, **update comments your change makes false**, match existing style/minimal diffs, never remove tests). Rule 4 is aimed straight at the stale-comment lie from the quality review. Six rules, not sixteen — the research was clear that instruction-following collapses with rule count on small models. Dynamic stuff (task, history) stays in the user turn, which also keeps the cacheable prefix stable.

Also applied from the research sweep: THINK now runs at Qwen's official thinking-mode sampling (temp 0.6 — the model card explicitly warns greedy decoding causes infinite loops), and DECIDE runs at temp 0 (extraction is classification; determinism is free accuracy). All 32 unit tests green.

Run 4 will tell us if the REFACTOR pass catches what the C+ run left behind.

content.text:
Short answer: include them, but **not as prompt text** — most of your universal rules should become enforcement, and the rest get progressive disclosure by phase. Dumping CODING-STEERING wholesale into the system prompt would be counterproductive: the research was unambiguous that instruction-following collapses with rule count on small models, and we just watched a 6-rule system prompt produce A-grade output where a 10-instruction task prompt produced flailing.

Here's the tiering I'd build, which matches how you already run things (structural enforcement over behavioral guidelines):

**Tier 1 — Guards, not words (zero prompt tokens).** Every rule that's mechanically checkable becomes a deterministic check in the loop, like the read-before-write guard and `ast.parse` lint gate already are:
- `SEC-001` no `eval`/`os.system`/`shell=True` → scan written content in the lint gate (the sandbox already blocks executing them; this catches *writing* them)
- `DPS-103` 500-line file cap → lint gate warning on write
- `TDD-001` red-before-green → already structural; the driver orders the phases and pytest is the gate
- `AI-003` minimal diffs → the read-before-write guard + write-echo already constrain this

A rule enforced by Python is followed 100% of the time at temperature anything. A rule in the prompt is followed ~90% on a good day.

**Tier 2 — Always-on system prompt (the 6 we have, cap ~8).** Only judgment-rules that apply to *every* write: complete-file fenced blocks, update stale comments, match existing style, never remove tests. These earn their tokens.

**Tier 3 — Phase-scoped injection (the progressive disclosure).** A small rules registry — each rule tagged with the phases it applies to — and the driver injects only the relevant 2-3 into that phase's task prompt:
- `act_red` gets TDD-002/004 (strong assertions, negative paths)
- `act_green` gets DPS-204 (no silent fallbacks, fail fast)
- `act_refactor` gets AI-003/004 (minimal diffs, preserve debug logs)
- review phases get the resiliency rules (timeouts, structured errors)

Selection is deterministic Python, not model judgment — the model never sees a rule it can't act on in the current step. That's the same principle as the Python boundary for file content: don't make the model carry what the harness can carry.

Rough shape: `rules.toml` with `{id, text, phases, enforcement: guard|prompt}`, the lint gate consumes the `guard` ones, `_build_think_prompt` appends the phase-matched `prompt` ones. ~50 lines plus tests.

- **run_id**: 20260610-202354
- **date**: 2026-06-10
- **context**: datum-local M1 — ReAct loop (`datum/agent_loop.py`) with

## Executive summary — what we adopted, what's backlog

### Adopted during M1 (same day)

| Finding | Source | Change |
|---|---|---|
| Architect/editor split is SOTA; freeform-then-extract is the published mitigation for constraint-induced reasoning loss | aider architect mode; Tam et al. 2408.02442 "NL-to-Format"; CRANE 2502.09061 | Validated `agent_loop.py` THINK/DECIDE design — kept |
| Whole-file fenced blocks beat diffs for Qwen3 (45.8% vs 41.3%, 100% vs 94.2% well-formed) | aider Qwen3 benchmark | Whole-file write_to_file as primary edit path |

| Finding | Source | Candidate change |

| Repair cap: edit-success drops 90.5% → 57.2% after first failure; gains concentrate in rounds 1-2 | SWE-agent; self-repair study 2604.10508 | Cap repair loops at 2, then force whole-file re-read + rewrite |

| Best-of-N patches filtered by test execution (+19 pts), nowhere else | CodeT 2207.10397; Agentless 2407.01489 | Sample 3-5 GREEN candidates at T=0.7, first passer wins |
| Evidence-first extraction schema: `quote_from_reasoning` before `tool_name`; enum tool names; `none` branch | Hammer 2410.04587; dottxt rebuttal | AgentDecision schema v2 |
| Hierarchical localization as its own phase (files → functions → edit sites) | Agentless | M2/M3 phase design |

---

## Report 1 — Edit formats for small/local models

(verbatim from research agent, 2026-06-10)

### Aider — the most rigorously benchmarked edit formats

**Sources:** [Edit formats](https://aider.chat/docs/more/edit-formats.html) · [Original benchmark](https://aider.chat/docs/benchmarks.html) · [Unified diffs post](https://aider.chat/2023/12/21/unified-diffs.html) · [Quantization post](https://aider.chat/2024/11/21/quantization.html) · [Qwen3 results](https://aider.chat/2025/05/08/qwen3.html) · [Architect/editor post](https://aider.chat/2024/09/26/architect.html) · [Edit-errors troubleshooting](https://aider.chat/docs/troubleshooting/edit-errors.html)

Formats: `whole` (full updated file, filename above a fenced block), `diff`
(search/replace blocks with git-merge-conflict markers), `diff-fenced`,
`udiff` (simplified unified diff, no line numbers), `editor-*` variants for
architect mode.

Benchmark findings:

- Plain-text formats beat JSON function-calling decisively; structured JSON
  degraded both format adherence and code quality. GPT-3.5: 46% `whole` vs
  ~19% `diff`. Weak models used diff pathologically (entire file in SEARCH).
- udiff: refactor benchmark 20% → 61% for GPT-4 Turbo. Models are bad with
  line numbers in any format (aider strips them; hunks applied by content
  matching). Disabling flexible patch application → 9X more edit errors.
  "High level diffs" prompting (replace whole functions) cut errors 30-50%.
- Quantization post (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, `diff`): 72.2% well-served vs 51.9%
  with 2k context defaults; well-formed-edit rate 95.5% → 46.2% purely from
  serving/template differences. Context window and chat template matter more
  than quantization.
- Qwen3-32B: **45.8% `whole` (100% well-formed) vs 41.3% `diff` (94.2%)**.
  Whole beat diff across Qwen3 sizes, even 235B. Sampling: /no_think,
  top_p 0.8, top_k 20, temp 0.7.
- Architect/editor split hit SOTA (85% o1-preview + cheap editor).
- Apply layer is layered: exact → whitespace-insensitive →
  indentation-preserving → difflib fuzzy; on failure send actual file
  content with "did you mean", resend only failed blocks.

### Cline — exact-match S/R blocks + state-sync guardrails

**Sources:** [Tools guide](https://docs.cline.bot/exploring-clines-tools/cline-tools-guide) · issues #2909, #3183, #4067, #4384

- `replace_in_file` uses SEARCH/REPLACE markers, exact character match, no
  fuzzy layer. `write_to_file` is the whole-file fallback.
- Key guardrail: every edit returns `final_file_content` (post-edit,
  post-auto-format) and the system prompt mandates using that as reference.
- Worst failure (#3183): on repeated S/R failure the model falls back to
  write_to_file and rewrites from hallucinated memory, corrupting the file.

### Roo Code — fuzzy matching with a position hint

**Sources:** [apply_diff](https://docs.roocode.com/features/tools/apply-diff) · [Code Surgery deep-dive](https://fabianhertwig.com/blog/coding-assistants-file-edits/)

- S/R blocks with mandatory `:start_line:` hint; middle-out fuzzy search
  within a 40-line buffer, Levenshtein scoring, configurable threshold.
- Indentation preservation: reapply the matched region's actual whitespace.
- Line hint narrows the search window but never decides the match.

### OpenHands — LLM-based draft editor

**Sources:** PR #3985 · issues #8112, #9920

- Default `str_replace_editor` breaks down past a few hundred lines.
- Draft editor: agent specifies line range + rough draft; second LLM
  regenerates the complete section (the Gemma-extractor pattern, validated
  in production). Alternative: whole-file generation, deterministic difflib
  diff, `patch` application.

### SWE-agent — guardrails quantified

**Sources:** [ACI paper 2405.15793](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.15793) · issue #560

- Lint gate on edits: removing it cost 3 points absolute (18% → 15%).
- 51.7% of GPT-4 Turbo trajectories contain a failed edit; eventual edit
  success 90.5%, but after one failure recovery odds drop to 57.2%.
- Lint the delta, not the file (pre-existing errors trap the agent).

### Honorable mentions

- OpenAI Codex V4A patch format: content anchors, never line numbers,
  progressive fallback matching, structured JSON error feedback.
- Cursor: custom-trained apply model integrates the main model's sketch.

---

## Report 2 — Constrained decoding, tiny-model extraction, context management, Qwen3 specifics

(verbatim from research agent, 2026-06-10)

### Does grammar-constrained decoding hurt reasoning?

- **"Let Me Speak Freely?" (Tam et al., arXiv:2408.02442)**: significant
  reasoning decline under format restrictions; stricter = worse. But
  classification/extraction tasks were unhurt or improved. Their NL-to-Format
  mitigation — natural language first, convert in a second pass — recovers
  most of the loss. That is exactly the THINK/DECIDE split.
- **dottxt "Say What You Mean" rebuttal**: with the schema shown in the
  prompt and a reasoning field before the answer field, structured generation
  matched or beat unstructured. Prescriptions: schema + example in prompt,
  bounded reasoning field first, enums/regex for the answer.
- **JSONSchemaBench (2501.10868)**: with adequate prompting, constrained
  decoding improved accuracy (+3.3 to +3.7 pp) and sped generation ~50%.
  Quality loss comes from poor schema/prompt design, not the constraint.
- **CRANE (ICML 2025, 2502.09061)**: theory — answer-only grammars provably
  reduce expressivity; adding a free reasoning region restores it (up to
  +10 pp). The field agrees reasoning must happen outside the grammar.

### Tool-call extraction with tiny models

- BFCL: Llama 3.1 8B ~76% AST-era; multi-turn is a cliff for small models.
- Docker eval (21 local models): Qwen3-8B F1 0.933, Gemma 3 4B 0.733.
  Failure modes in order: eager invocation, wrong tool, invalid args,
  ignoring tool responses. Quantization had no significant effect.
  95% per-step accuracy → ~66% over 8 steps.
- Hammer (2410.04587): small models are misled by function/parameter names;
  weak at irrelevance detection. Name masking + irrelevance training helps.
- Reframing decision→extraction moves the task from hard-for-4B
  function-calling to easy-for-4B constrained extraction.

### Multi-turn context management

- **"The Complexity Trap" (2508.21433, JetBrains)**: simple observation
  masking (full observations last M=10 turns, one-line placeholders older,
  keep ALL reasoning/action tokens) matches or beats LLM summarization at
  ~half the cost. Summaries mask failure signals → agents persist in dead
  ends. Masking is the default for 30B-class local models.
- SWE-agent ships observation masking; OpenHands uses an LLM condenser
  (inherits the failure-signal problem, needs a second model call).

### Qwen3-30B-A3B specifics

| | Original (hybrid) | Instruct-2507 | Thinking-2507 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sampling | think: T=0.6/top_p 0.95/top_k 20; no_think: T=0.7/top_p 0.8 | T=0.7/top_p 0.8 | T=0.6/top_p 0.95 |
| Context | 32K native (YaRN→128K) | 256K | 256K |
| BFCL-v3 | 69.1 (thinking) | 65.1 | 72.4 |

- Never greedy-decode thinking mode (endless repetitions per model card).
- Thinking beats no_think for tool decisions on this family (72.4 vs 65.1).
- Exclude `<think>` content from multi-turn history (official requirement).
- Qwen-Agent framework has battle-tested tool-call templates worth mining.

---

## Report 3 — Fully-local autonomous coding pipelines

(verbatim from research agent, 2026-06-10)

### What 30B-class local models achieve

- Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B: 50.3% SWE-bench Verified; a fine-tune of the general
  Qwen3-30B-A3B matches it. Realistic ceiling for the class with a good
  scaffold. Stock 30B-A3B lands meaningfully lower.
- Devstral-Small (24B) + OpenHands: 46.8% SWE-bench Verified, beating much
  larger models under the same scaffold — model+harness co-design beats
  parameter count.
- Terminal-Bench 2.0: the same model swings 30-50 points depending on
  harness. The scaffold is worth more than a model upgrade.
- gpt-engineer / Devika: no quantitative local-model success data exists.
- smolagents CodeAgent (actions as Python code): ~30% fewer steps.

### TDD loops and execution feedback

- Tests-in-prompt: MBPP 69.67% → 82.45%, HumanEval 78.66% → 87.81%
  (Mathews & Nagappan, 2402.13521). Replicated on Llama 3.
- Iterative self-repair with execution errors (2604.10508): +4.9 to +17.1
  HumanEval, +16.0 to +30.0 MBPP across scales; gains concentrate in the
  first two repair rounds; modern instruction-tuned small models self-repair
  without fine-tuning. Strongest direct evidence the RED-GREEN loop with
  pytest as verifier is correct for a 30B.
- Caveat (2602.07900): agent-written mid-task tests correlate weakly with
  success and drift to print-debugging. Value is in tests generated in a
  dedicated gated phase then frozen as the verifier.

### Self-consistency / voting

- CodeT (2207.10397): +18.8 absolute via dual execution agreement on final
  artifacts. Agentless samples candidate patches, selects via tests.
- Intermediate-step voting: not worth single-stream local latency. Spend
  samples only where a deterministic verifier exists.

### Pipeline-of-small-steps vs monolithic agent

- Agentless (2407.01489): fixed three-phase pipeline beat every open-source
  agent on SWE-bench Lite (32.0%) at $0.70/issue. The weaker the model, the
  stronger the case for removing action-selection from it.
- Small Agent Collaboration (2601.11327): 4B with tools (18.2%) beat 32B
  without (12.7%); full thinking mode frequently degraded agentic
  performance (tool omission, looping, format drift); best results with
  thinking only in the planning role.
- Every degree of freedom removed from a sub-70B model converts directly
  into reliability.

| Evidence-first extraction schema: `quote_from_reasoning` before `tool_name`; enum tool names; `none` branch | Hammer 2410.04587; dottxt rebuttal | AgentDecision schema v2 |

## Report 1 — Edit formats for small/local models

(verbatim from research agent, 2026-06-10)

### Aider — the most rigorously benchmarked edit formats

**Sources:** [Edit formats](https://aider.chat/docs/more/edit-formats.html) · [Original benchmark](https://aider.chat/docs/benchmarks.html) · [Unified diffs post](https://aider.chat/2023/12/21/unified-diffs.html) · [Quantization post](https://aider.chat/2024/11/21/quantization.html) · [Qwen3 results](https://aider.chat/2025/05/08/qwen3.html) · [Architect/editor post](https://aider.chat/2024/09/26/architect.html) · [Edit-errors troubleshooting](https://aider.chat/docs/troubleshooting/edit-errors.html)

Formats: `whole` (full updated file, filename above a fenced block), `diff`
(search/replace blocks with git-merge-conflict markers), `diff-fenced`,
`udiff` (simplified unified diff, no line numbers), `editor-*` variants for
architect mode.

Benchmark findings:

- Plain-text formats beat JSON function-calling decisively; structured JSON
  degraded both format adherence and code quality. GPT-3.5: 46% `whole` vs
  ~19% `diff`. Weak models used diff pathologically (entire file in SEARCH).
- udiff: refactor benchmark 20% → 61% for GPT-4 Turbo. Models are bad with
  line numbers in any format (aider strips them; hunks applied by content
  matching). Disabling flexible patch application → 9X more edit errors.
  "High level diffs" prompting (replace whole functions) cut errors 30-50%.
- Quantization post (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, `diff`): 72.2% well-served vs 51.9%
  with 2k context defaults; well-formed-edit rate 95.5% → 46.2% purely from
  serving/template differences. Context window and chat template matter more
  than quantization.
- Qwen3-32B: **45.8% `whole` (100% well-formed) vs 41.3% `diff` (94.2%)**.
  Whole beat diff across Qwen3 sizes, even 235B. Sampling: /no_think,
  top_p 0.8, top_k 20, temp 0.7.
- Architect/editor split hit SOTA (85% o1-preview + cheap editor).
- Apply layer is layered: exact → whitespace-insensitive →
  indentation-preserving → difflib fuzzy; on failure send actual file
  content with "did you mean", resend only failed blocks.

### Cline — exact-match S/R blocks + state-sync guardrails

**Sources:** [Tools guide](https://docs.cline.bot/exploring-clines-tools/cline-tools-guide) · issues #2909, #3183, #4067, #4384

- `replace_in_file` uses SEARCH/REPLACE markers, exact character match, no
  fuzzy layer. `write_to_file` is the whole-file fallback.
- Key guardrail: every edit returns `final_file_content` (post-edit,
  post-auto-format) and the system prompt mandates using that as reference.
- Worst failure (#3183): on repeated S/R failure the model falls back to
  write_to_file and rewrites from hallucinated memory, corrupting the file.

### Roo Code — fuzzy matching with a position hint

**Sources:** [apply_diff](https://docs.roocode.com/features/tools/apply-diff) · [Code Surgery deep-dive](https://fabianhertwig.com/blog/coding-assistants-file-edits/)

- S/R blocks with mandatory `:start_line:` hint; middle-out fuzzy search
  within a 40-line buffer, Levenshtein scoring, configurable threshold.
- Indentation preservation: reapply the matched region's actual whitespace.
- Line hint narrows the search window but never decides the match.

### OpenHands — LLM-based draft editor

**Sources:** PR #3985 · issues #8112, #9920

- Default `str_replace_editor` breaks down past a few hundred lines.
- Draft editor: agent specifies line range + rough draft; second LLM
  regenerates the complete section (the Gemma-extractor pattern, validated
  in production). Alternative: whole-file generation, deterministic difflib
  diff, `patch` application.

### SWE-agent — guardrails quantified

**Sources:** [ACI paper 2405.15793](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.15793) · issue #560

- Lint gate on edits: removing it cost 3 points absolute (18% → 15%).
- 51.7% of GPT-4 Turbo trajectories contain a failed edit; eventual edit
  success 90.5%, but after one failure recovery odds drop to 57.2%.
- Lint the delta, not the file (pre-existing errors trap the agent).

### Honorable mentions

- OpenAI Codex V4A patch format: content anchors, never line numbers,
  progressive fallback matching, structured JSON error feedback.
- Cursor: custom-trained apply model integrates the main model's sketch.

---

## Report 2 — Constrained decoding, tiny-model extraction, context management, Qwen3 specifics

(verbatim from research agent, 2026-06-10)

### Does grammar-constrained decoding hurt reasoning?

- **"Let Me Speak Freely?" (Tam et al., arXiv:2408.02442)**: significant
  reasoning decline under format restrictions; stricter = worse. But
  classification/extraction tasks were unhurt or improved. Their NL-to-Format
  mitigation — natural language first, convert in a second pass — recovers
  most of the loss. That is exactly the THINK/DECIDE split.
- **dottxt "Say What You Mean" rebuttal**: with the schema shown in the
  prompt and a reasoning field before the answer field, structured generation
  matched or beat unstructured. Prescriptions: schema + example in prompt,
  bounded reasoning field first, enums/regex for the answer.
- **JSONSchemaBench (2501.10868)**: with adequate prompting, constrained
  decoding improved accuracy (+3.3 to +3.7 pp) and sped generation ~50%.
  Quality loss comes from poor schema/prompt design, not the constraint.
- **CRANE (ICML 2025, 2502.09061)**: theory — answer-only grammars provably
  reduce expressivity; adding a free reasoning region restores it (up to
  +10 pp). The field agrees reasoning must happen outside the grammar.

### Tool-call extraction with tiny models

- BFCL: Llama 3.1 8B ~76% AST-era; multi-turn is a cliff for small models.
- Docker eval (21 local models): Qwen3-8B F1 0.933, Gemma 3 4B 0.733.
  Failure modes in order: eager invocation, wrong tool, invalid args,
  ignoring tool responses. Quantization had no significant effect.
  95% per-step accuracy → ~66% over 8 steps.
- Hammer (2410.04587): small models are misled by function/parameter names;
  weak at irrelevance detection. Name masking + irrelevance training helps.
- Reframing decision→extraction moves the task from hard-for-4B
  function-calling to easy-for-4B constrained extraction.

### Multi-turn context management

- **"The Complexity Trap" (2508.21433, JetBrains)**: simple observation
  masking (full observations last M=10 turns, one-line placeholders older,
  keep ALL reasoning/action tokens) matches or beats LLM summarization at
  ~half the cost. Summaries mask failure signals → agents persist in dead
  ends. Masking is the default for 30B-class local models.
- SWE-agent ships observation masking; OpenHands uses an LLM condenser
  (inherits the failure-signal problem, needs a second model call).

### Qwen3-30B-A3B specifics

| | Original (hybrid) | Instruct-2507 | Thinking-2507 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sampling | think: T=0.6/top_p 0.95/top_k 20; no_think: T=0.7/top_p 0.8 | T=0.7/top_p 0.8 | T=0.6/top_p 0.95 |
| Context | 32K native (YaRN→128K) | 256K | 256K |
| BFCL-v3 | 69.1 (thinking) | 65.1 | 72.4 |

- Never greedy-decode thinking mode (endless repetitions per model card).
- Thinking beats no_think for tool decisions on this family (72.4 vs 65.1).
- Exclude `<think>` content from multi-turn history (official requirement).
- Qwen-Agent framework has battle-tested tool-call templates worth mining.

---

## Report 3 — Fully-local autonomous coding pipelines

(verbatim from research agent, 2026-06-10)

### What 30B-class local models achieve

- Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B: 50.3% SWE-bench Verified; a fine-tune of the general
  Qwen3-30B-A3B matches it. Realistic ceiling for the class with a good
  scaffold. Stock 30B-A3B lands meaningfully lower.
- Devstral-Small (24B) + OpenHands: 46.8% SWE-bench Verified, beating much
  larger models under the same scaffold — model+harness co-design beats
  parameter count.
- Terminal-Bench 2.0: the same model swings 30-50 points depending on
  harness. The scaffold is worth more than a model upgrade.
- gpt-engineer / Devika: no quantitative local-model success data exists.
- smolagents CodeAgent (actions as Python code): ~30% fewer steps.

### TDD loops and execution feedback

- Tests-in-prompt: MBPP 69.67% → 82.45%, HumanEval 78.66% → 87.81%
  (Mathews & Nagappan, 2402.13521). Replicated on Llama 3.
- Iterative self-repair with execution errors (2604.10508): +4.9 to +17.1
  HumanEval, +16.0 to +30.0 MBPP across scales; gains concentrate in the
  first two repair rounds; modern instruction-tuned small models self-repair
  without fine-tuning. Strongest direct evidence the RED-GREEN loop with
  pytest as verifier is correct for a 30B.
- Caveat (2602.07900): agent-written mid-task tests correlate weakly with
  success and drift to print-debugging. Value is in tests generated in a
  dedicated gated phase then frozen as the verifier.

### Self-consistency / voting

- CodeT (2207.10397): +18.8 absolute via dual execution agreement on final
  artifacts. Agentless samples candidate patches, selects via tests.
- Intermediate-step voting: not worth single-stream local latency. Spend
  samples only where a deterministic verifier exists.

### Pipeline-of-small-steps vs monolithic agent

- Agentless (2407.01489): fixed three-phase pipeline beat every open-source
  agent on SWE-bench Lite (32.0%) at $0.70/issue. The weaker the model, the
  stronger the case for removing action-selection from it.
- Small Agent Collaboration (2601.11327): 4B with tools (18.2%) beat 32B
  without (12.7%); full thinking mode frequently degraded agentic
  performance (tool omission, looping, format drift); best results with
  thinking only in the planning role.
- Every degree of freedom removed from a sub-70B model converts directly
  into reliability.

1	# Agent Persona: Critical Collaborator
2	
3	All agents operating in this repository must adhere strictly to the following interaction constraints.
4	
5	## Core Directives
6	1. **No Hype:** Strip all enthusiastic filler ("Awesome", "Love it", "Holy grail", "Great idea"). Treat the user as a peer engineer, not someone to flatter.
7	2. **Push Back:** Assume proposed architectures have flaws. Highlight edge cases, coupling risks, and maintenance burdens before agreeing to build them.
8	3. **Neutral Tone:** Keep responses analytical, detached, and focused strictly on the technical tradeoffs.
9	4. **Answer Directly:** Do not pad responses with validation. State the facts, present the tradeoffs, and ask for the technical decision.
10	5. **Tasks Always Active:** When running DATUM, ALWAYS maintain tasks via TaskCreate/TaskUpdate. Create a task for each pipeline phase and each Act lane. Mark `in_progress` when starting, `completed` when done. The task list is the live status board — if a user asks "where are we", the task list answers it. Never ignore the task tool reminders.
11	6. **Local LLM = Subagent Only:** When a pipeline phase uses local Gemma inference, ALWAYS spawn a subagent (Agent tool with `model: "sonnet"`) that imports and calls `datum.local_llm.run_phase()` from Python. NEVER invoke `datum local-llm` via Bash. The subagent handles the inference, checks the `escalated` flag, and returns the result. If `escalated=True`, the orchestrator retries with Claude. The `datum local-llm` CLI exists for human testing at the terminal — agents must not use it.
12	
13	## Local LLM — Multi-Turn Orchestration
14	
15	`run_phase()` auto-routes to multi-turn mode when `[multi_turn]` is enabled for a phase
16	in `config.toml`. The flow:
17	
18	1. **Planning turn** — Gemma analyzes the problem, outputs a `StepPlan` (list of actions)
19	2. **Execution turns** — Gemma executes each step, outputs `StepResult` with confidence score
20	3. **Synthesis turn** — Gemma combines all findings into the phase's final schema
21	
22	### Escalation rules
23	
24	- If any turn triggers repetition, context overflow, or the model says `ESCALATE` → escalate to Claude
25	- If confidence stays below `confidence_threshold` after retries → escalate
26	- If total wall-clock exceeds `timeout_s` → escalate
27	- The orchestrator retries with Claude using the accumulated context as a head start
28	
29	### Key parameters (all in `config.toml` under `[multi_turn]`)
30	
31	| Parameter | Default | What it does |
32	|-----------|---------|-------------|
33	| `max_turns` | 5 | Max reasoning turns before forced escalation |
34	| `timeout_s` | 300 | Total wall-clock budget for all turns |
35	| `turn_timeout_s` | 90 | Max wall-clock per individual turn |
36	| `confidence_threshold` | 0.8 | Exit early when confidence >= this |
37	| `temperature_schedule` | fixed | `fixed` / `rising` / `falling` / `u_curve` |
38	| `context_reserve_pct` | 20 | % of context window reserved for synthesis |
39	| `retry_on_low_confidence` | true | Retry a turn if confidence < threshold |
40	| `max_retries_per_turn` | 2 | Max retries per turn before accepting best |
41	| `planning_turn` | true | Turn 0 produces a step plan |
42	| `verification_turn` | true | Final turn synthesizes into phase schema |
43	
44	Per-phase overrides go in `[multi_turn.phase_overrides.<phase>]`.
45	
46	### Subagent pattern
47	
48	```python
49	from datum.local_llm import run_phase
50	
51	result = run_phase(
52	    phase="triage",
53	    prompt=prompt_text,
54	    schema=TriageDecision,
55	    mt_overrides={"max_turns": 3}
56	)
57	
58	if result["escalated"]:
59	    # retry with Claude, pass result["turns"] as context
60	    ...
61	else:
62	    answer = result["result"]
63	```
64	
65	## Self-Healing: Auto-File Bugs
66	
67	When DATUM hits an **unexpected** error during execution — script crash, missing file the pipeline expected to exist, schema validation failure on a file DATUM itself wrote, subprocess exit code != 0 on a DATUM script — the agent MUST file a GitHub issue before continuing or halting.
68	
69	**What qualifies as a bug (file it):**
70	- A DATUM script (`gate.py`, `lane_plan.py`, `classify.py`, etc.) crashes with a traceback
71	- A gate fails on an artifact DATUM itself generated (not user-authored)
72	- A file referenced in SKILL.md or a reference doc doesn't exist
73	- `datum doctor` or `datum status` returns an error
74	
75	**What is NOT a bug (don't file it):**
76	- A gate fails because the user hasn't filled in an artifact yet (expected behavior)
77	- Tests fail on user code (that's the pipeline working correctly)
78	- The user cancels or overrides a phase
79	
80	**How to file:**
81	```bash
82	datum bugfile <module> "<one-line description>" --trace "<traceback>"
83	```
84	
85	This deduplicates against open issues, attaches the current `.datum/state.json` snapshot, and labels with `datum-bug`. Agents and scripts can also call `datum.report_bug.report_bug(module, error, context)` directly from Python.
86	
87	**Then:** Continue if the error is non-fatal (log it and proceed). Halt if fatal (missing script, broken state).
88

5. **Tasks Always Active:** When running DATUM, ALWAYS maintain tasks via TaskCreate/TaskUpdate. Create a task for each pipeline phase and each Act lane. Mark `in_progress` when starting, `completed` when done. The task list is the live status board — if a user asks "where are we", the task list answers it. Never ignore the task tool reminders.
6. **Local LLM = Subagent Only:** When a pipeline phase uses local Gemma inference, ALWAYS spawn a subagent (Agent tool with `model: "sonnet"`) that imports and calls `datum.local_llm.run_phase()` from Python. NEVER invoke `datum local-llm` via Bash. The subagent handles the inference, checks the `escalated` flag, and returns the result. If `escalated=True`, the orchestrator retries with Claude. The `datum local-llm` CLI exists for human testing at the terminal — agents must not use it.

## Local LLM — Multi-Turn Orchestration

`run_phase()` auto-routes to multi-turn mode when `[multi_turn]` is enabled for a phase
in `config.toml`. The flow:

1. **Planning turn** — Gemma analyzes the problem, outputs a `StepPlan` (list of actions)
2. **Execution turns** — Gemma executes each step, outputs `StepResult` with confidence score
3. **Synthesis turn** — Gemma combines all findings into the phase's final schema

### Escalation rules

- If any turn triggers repetition, context overflow, or the model says `ESCALATE` → escalate to Claude
- If confidence stays below `confidence_threshold` after retries → escalate
- If total wall-clock exceeds `timeout_s` → escalate
- The orchestrator retries with Claude using the accumulated context as a head start

### Key parameters (all in `config.toml` under `[multi_turn]`)

| Parameter | Default | What it does |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| `max_turns` | 5 | Max reasoning turns before forced escalation |
| `timeout_s` | 300 | Total wall-clock budget for all turns |
| `turn_timeout_s` | 90 | Max wall-clock per individual turn |
| `confidence_threshold` | 0.8 | Exit early when confidence >= this |
| `temperature_schedule` | fixed | `fixed` / `rising` / `falling` / `u_curve` |
| `context_reserve_pct` | 20 | % of context window reserved for synthesis |
| `retry_on_low_confidence` | true | Retry a turn if confidence < threshold |
| `max_retries_per_turn` | 2 | Max retries per turn before accepting best |
| `planning_turn` | true | Turn 0 produces a step plan |
| `verification_turn` | true | Final turn synthesizes into phase schema |

Per-phase overrides go in `[multi_turn.phase_overrides.<phase>]`.

### Subagent pattern

```python
from datum.local_llm import run_phase

result = run_phase(
    phase="triage",
    prompt=prompt_text,
    schema=TriageDecision,
    mt_overrides={"max_turns": 3}
)

if result["escalated"]:
    # retry with Claude, pass result["turns"] as context
    ...
else:
    answer = result["result"]
```

## Self-Healing: Auto-File Bugs

When DATUM hits an **unexpected** error during execution — script crash, missing file the pipeline expected to exist, schema validation failure on a file DATUM itself wrote, subprocess exit code != 0 on a DATUM script — the agent MUST file a GitHub issue before continuing or halting.

**What qualifies as a bug (file it):**
- A DATUM script (`gate.py`, `lane_plan.py`, `classify.py`, etc.) crashes with a traceback
- A gate fails on an artifact DATUM itself generated (not user-authored)
- A file referenced in SKILL.md or a reference doc doesn't exist
- `datum doctor` or `datum status` returns an error

**What is NOT a bug (don't file it):**
- A gate fails because the user hasn't filled in an artifact yet (expected behavior)
- Tests fail on user code (that's the pipeline working correctly)
- The user cancels or overrides a phase

**How to file:**
```bash
datum bugfile <module> "<one-line description>" --trace "<traceback>"
```

This deduplicates against open issues, attaches the current `.datum/state.json` snapshot, and labels with `datum-bug`. Agents and scripts can also call `datum.report_bug.report_bug(module, error, context)` directly from Python.

**Then:** Continue if the error is non-fatal (log it and proceed). Halt if fatal (missing script, broken state).

# ── Lint gate: banned constructs, size, swallowed errors, /tmp ──────────────


def _write_and_run(thought_content, path="f.py"):
    """Run one write step with the given fenced content; return observation."""
    with (
        patch(
            "datum.agent_loop._think",
            _mk_think([f"write\n```\n{thought_content}\n```", "done"]),
        ),
        patch(
            "datum.agent_loop._decide",
            _mk_decide(
                [
                    {"action": "tool", "tool_name": "write_to_file",
                     "tool_args": {"path": path}},
                    {"action": "done", "summary": "ok"},
                ]
            ),
        ),
        patch("datum.agent_loop._execute_tool", lambda tc, cfg: ('{"ok": true}', False)),
    ):
        result = agent_loop("task", BASE_CFG, phase="act_red")
    return result["steps"][0]["observation"]


def test_lint_flags_eval(tmp_path, monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.chdir(tmp_path)
    obs = _write_and_run("x = eval(user_input)")
    assert "eval" in obs and "WARNING" in obs


def test_lint_flags_os_system(tmp_path, monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.chdir(tmp_path)
    obs = _write_and_run("import os\nos.system('ls')")
    assert "os.system" in obs and "WARNING" in obs


def test_lint_flags_shell_true(tmp_path, monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.chdir(tmp_path)
    obs = _write_and_run(

    )
    assert "shell=True" in obs and "WARNING" in obs


def test_lint_flags_bare_except_pass(tmp_path, monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.chdir(tmp_path)
    obs = _write_and_run("try:\n    f()\nexcept:\n    pass")
    assert "except" in obs and "WARNING" in obs


def test_lint_flags_tmp_path(tmp_path, monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.chdir(tmp_path)

def test_lint_flags_oversized_file(tmp_path, monkeypatch):

- **Self-review with the project's own tool before handback** (eedom): run the linter/reviewer the repo ships against your own diff; loop until clean. Generalizes to any repo with a quality tool.

- **Never run `go test -v`** (fastDelete): property-based test output floods/crashes terminals — an instance of a general "cap tool output verbosity" rule.

- **Backup compliance** (the-record-infra): adding any service with a persistent DB requires updating the backup script in the same change — "feature must carry its operational obligations."
- **Advisory-only / read-only API allowlist** (power-scp-optimizer): explicit enumerated allowlist of permitted API calls; all mutations forbidden. Strong pattern for any cloud-touching agent.

- **Non-Pushy Rule** (the-record-suite): when the human is exploring/asking questions, do not push toward implementation, commits, or sprints.
- **Active TODO mandatory** (the-record-suite): task list never goes empty mid-session — "a session with no tasks is a session with no visibility."

- **Port discipline** (baGuy): "Never run this app on port 3000 for local testing" — environment-collision rule.
- **Requirements syntax standard** (baGuy): JTBD elicitation + EARS sentence patterns + Given/When/Then acceptance criteria.
- **Skill descriptions must describe what users say, not what the tool does; min 80 chars** (ee-skills) — anti-undertriggering rule.
- **Never set versions manually — derive from commit prefixes via tooling** (ecTUI/svu).
- **Never use `~` in code — `Path.home()` / `${HOME}`** (podlead).
- **No meeting/user content in telemetry; explicit OSLog privacy labels on every interpolation** (the-record-suite) — privacy-by-construction.

1. **`claude/*` branches.** ecTUI: "Develop on `claude/*` branches" vs fcc/CLAUDE.md: "Never use `claude/` as a branch prefix", wfc/baGuy: "No AI-revealing prefixes / NEVER reveal AI tool names in branches." ecTUI is the outlier (likely predates the no-leakage policy).
2. **Squash vs append-only.** Global `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` ("Always squash all local commits into one before pushing. One commit per PR. No exceptions.") and ee-skills ("Squash merge — one commit per PR") vs wfc/CLAUDE.md: "Complete PRs **without** squash-merging (MUST)... Force-pushes and remote-branch squashing are forbidden." WFC permits squashing only *before first push*. Direct policy conflict for any repo where both apply.
3. **`from __future__ import annotations`.** podlead: required "in every file" vs power-scp-optimizer: "no `from __future__ import annotations`" (use native `X | Y`, `type` aliases). Per-project, but contradictory as universal candidates.
4. **HTTP client.** podlead: "`requests` for HTTP. No httpx, no aiohttp" vs global CODING-STEERING PY-001 toolchain: `httpx`.

6. **`refactor:` bump semantics.** ecTUI: `refactor:` → patch bump vs eedom/ee-skills: refactors are `chore:`/no bump. Minor versioning drift.
7. **Grep usage.** GitNexus-bearing repos: "use `gitnexus_query` instead of grepping" vs files like fastDelete/ecTUI that assume normal search. Not a true conflict, but enforcement scope is inconsistent across repos.

## 4. Notable Enforcement Patterns from Third-Party Files (mechanisms only)

From **gitnexus/AGENTS.md**:
- **Versioned, changelogged instruction file** — semver header, "Last reviewed" date, changelog table. Treats the rules file as a maintained artifact with drift detection.
- **Scope table** — explicit Reads / Writes / Executes / Off-limits boundary matrix per repo.
- **Context-dilution countermeasure** — instructs the agent that on long threads the phrase "Remember: apply all AGENTS.md rules" re-weights instructions.
- **Hook-blocked commits** — PreToolUse hook blocks `git_commit` until `npm test` passes; enforcement in the harness, not the prose.
- **Context budget discipline** — split always-on rules into glob-scoped `.cursor/rules/*.mdc`; load `STANDARDS.md` only when needed.
- **Model pinning** — require a named/versioned model; ban `Auto`/`latest` when reproducibility matters.
- **Self-check exit checklist** — a numbered "before finishing" verification list the agent must walk.

From **SuperClaude_Framework/AGENTS.md**:
- **Make targets as the canonical interface** — `make doctor`/`make verify` health checks wired into the workflow, so agents probe environment validity deterministically.
- **Pytest markers mapped to features in `pyproject.toml`** — taxonomy enforced by config, not convention.
- **Coverage scope enforced by config** — "adjust configuration instead of skipping logic."
- **Pre-PR command gauntlet stated as a fixed list** (`make lint && make format && make test`) with required verification summary in the PR description.

## 5. Rules Specifically About CODE the Agent Writes

These are the rules a code-writing agent's enforcement registry should carry (vs orchestration/workflow rules above):

**Structure & architecture**
- Strict layer/tier import boundaries; cross-tier only via interfaces/protocol seams (7 files)
- File size caps: 500 lines hard, or per-layer 100–300 (3 files)
- No abstractions until second concrete use; KISS; "elegant means obvious" — readable names, straight-line data flow, small functions (baGuy)
- Repository pattern for all data access; never call cloud SDKs from UI/service code (ecTUI)
- Domain layer holds all types/enums/constants — never duplicate them (power-scp-optimizer)

**Error handling & data**
- No silent fallbacks: never `??`/`||` masking missing data — throw (baGuy, newDrug, +global)
- No catch-all try/catch; errors propagate, catch only at boundaries (baGuy)
- Fail loud with actionable context — no empty-array/placeholder/best-effort hiding (baGuy)
- Validate shape at every boundary: Zod/Pydantic on all incoming payloads (baGuy, SGF, newDrug, +global)
- Translate all external errors to domain errors at the infrastructure boundary (the-record-suite)
- Idempotent writes (`INSERT OR IGNORE`) wherever persistence is touched (the-record-suite, +global DPS-201)

**Language-specific**
- Python: 3.12+, Pydantic v2, uv-run-only, ruff; never `~` in paths — `Path.home()` (podlead, power-scp, insights)
- Swift: actors for shared mutable state, `@MainActor` presentation, `@Observable` not ObservableObject, no `@unchecked Sendable` outside audio, weak self in ViewModel Tasks, OSLog privacy labels on every interpolation (the-record-suite, .cursorrules)
- Go: `sync/atomic` for counters not mutexes; platform code behind build tags; context.Context first param everywhere (fastDelete, ecTUI)
- JS/React: ES modules, function components + hooks, PascalCase components / camelCase state / UPPER_SNAKE constants; shared visual values in CSS custom properties (baGuy)
- CSS: no hardcoded colors outside `:root` tokens (SGF)

**Tests as code**
- Assert concrete business outcomes, not existence (baGuy, +global TDD-002)
- Property tests for invariants + unit tests for cases; never hardcode iteration counts (fastDelete, ecTUI, podlead)
- Colocate tests beside the module; `tested-by:` annotation per source file (baGuy, eedom)
- Test count never decreases; full-suite regression after every change (the-record-suite, eedom)

**Honesty constraints**
- No invented API surface — never call methods/options/imports not confirmed to exist (baGuy, +global AI-002)
- Minimal diffs — change only what the task requires; no drive-by rewrites; no logic changes during structural refactors (baGuy, the-record-suite, gitnexus, +global AI-003)
- No fake logic / hardcoded returns to pass tests (+global TDD-003)
- No hardcoded secrets, org-specific values, or env-specific URLs in source (podlead, the-record-infra, baGuy)
